items.label: f01-pagesize-or-zero
items.front: Settings code reads `const pageSize = settings.pageSize || 10;` and a user has saved `pageSize: 0`. What does the app use, and why?
items.back: It uses 10: 0 is falsy, so || discards the user's value. Fix: `settings.pageSize ?? 10`, which falls back only on null/undefined. Keep || for real boolean logic.

items.label: f04-delete-204-json
items.front: A deletePost helper ends with `return res.json();` after a DELETE. Deletes succeed on the server but the UI shows an error every time. What is happening?
items.back: DELETE often returns 204 No Content; parsing an empty body as JSON throws, turning a successful delete into a failure. Fix: check res.ok and do not parse the body of a DELETE (or check for 204 first).

items.label: f03-fetch-no-res-ok
items.front: A getTodo helper does `const res = await fetch(url); return res.json();` with a .catch on the caller. For a missing id the server answers 404, yet the catch never fires. Why?
items.back: fetch only rejects on network failure; a 404/500 still resolves. Without `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...)` the error body is parsed as data. Fix: check res.ok before res.json().

items.label: f02-shallow-copy-nested
items.front: Code copies a profile with `const shallow = { ...original }` and then sets `shallow.address.city = "NYC"`. A bug report says the original profile's city changed too. Why?
items.back: Spread copies one level; `address` is a shared nested object, so the write lands in both. Fix: `structuredClone(original)` (or copy the nested level too) when the copy must be independent.

Nothing at all, as JSON.stringify throws as soon as an object contains a function value
All three keys come back, with `fn` turned into its source text and `missing` turned into null
Only `date` survives, as an ISO string, not a Date, while the function and undefined key drop

items.prompt: updatePost sends only `{ title: "Edited" }`. Why does the lab use PATCH for that request rather than PUT?

choices.text: PATCH is idempotent and PUT is not, so a retried PUT could end up applying the title change twice
PUT cannot carry a JSON body, so the new title would have to be moved into the query string instead
PATCH changes only the fields sent, while PUT replaces the whole resource with the body
PUT is reserved for creating new resources, so it would add a second post instead of editing one

PATCH changes only the fields sent, while PUT replaces the whole resource with the body
PUT is reserved for creating new resources, so it would add a second post instead of editing one

items.explanation: Problem 31: PATCH = change only these fields; PUT = replace the whole resource. CRUD: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE.

items.prompt: In fetchWithRetry, what would the caller observe if the final `throw lastError;` were deleted and every attempt failed?

choices.text: It resolves undefined: .then throws reading todo.title, so .catch logs a TypeError instead
Node would crash with an unhandled rejection: the errors were caught inside the loop but never logged
The loop would retry forever: nothing would stop it once the three attempts were used up
The last error would still reach .catch: the catch block inside the loop already rethrows it

choices: It resolves undefined: .then throws reading todo.title, so .catch logs a TypeError instead
Node would crash with an unhandled rejection: the errors were caught inside the loop but never logged
The loop would retry forever: nothing would stop it once the three attempts were used up
The last error would still reach .catch: the catch block inside the loop already rethrows it

items.explanation: Problem 32: the catch inside the loop swallows each failure (lastError = err); `throw lastError` after the loop is what surfaces the final error once all attempts are exhausted. Without it the function resolves undefined, the caller's `.then((todo) => console.log(todo.title))` throws a TypeError reading `title`, and `.catch` logs that TypeError instead of the HTTP error.

filter is faster than splice here, as it skips the index lookup that splice needs before removing
splice cannot remove an item by its id, only by value, so it would end up deleting the wrong todo
filter deep-clones each remaining todo, so later edits to the new list cannot reach the old objects

Returning false reports that nothing was deleted and leaves it to the caller whether that is an error
remove cannot throw, as filter swallows any exception that is raised inside its callback function

items.prompt: A page loads three users with `await Promise.all([...])` and one request rejects. What does the page get, and which tool keeps the two successful users?

choices.text: Promise.all retries the failed request once and then resolves; Promise.allSettled skips the retry and rejects
Promise.all waits for all three, then rejects with an array of errors; Promise.allSettled would throw sooner
Promise.all rejects with that error and gives no results; Promise.allSettled reports each outcome, keeping the two
Promise.all resolves with the two users plus an undefined slot; Promise.allSettled would only add the error message

items.explanation: Problem 28: if ANY promise rejects, Promise.all rejects immediately with that error; allSettled returns fulfilled/rejected records you can filter.

items.prompt: `timer.start()` passes `function () { console.log(this.seconds); }` to setTimeout and logs undefined. Why does switching the callback to an arrow function fix it?

choices.text: Arrow functions run synchronously inside start(), so they read `this.seconds` before the timer ever fires
Arrow functions are automatically bound to the object literal they are written in, just like a class method
An arrow function has no `this` of its own, so it inherits start()'s `this`, which is the timer object
setTimeout calls arrow callbacks with the original object as an argument instead of as `this`

setTimeout calls arrow callbacks with the original object as an argument instead of as `this`

items.explanation: Problem 23: `this` is set by how a function is called (the timer machinery calls the plain function); arrows capture `this` lexically. `.bind(this)` is the other fix.

Faster than Promise.all: consecutive awaits avoid the overhead of combining three promises

`let` is block-scoped, so each iteration gets its own binding and each callback keeps the value from its pass
`let` copies the counter into each callback at creation time, while `var` passes it by reference to the callback
